messages:
tasha: FYI, new dev onboard hit a weird hang pattern when using the Go Generator in an HTTP handler. not identical to previous threads tested different sample app layout and saw similar goroutine pileup but with a different touch: we spawn a worker per-request that proxies stream chunks to a websocket, and sometimes the worker never exits after client disconnects.

ben: can you paste the worker sketch? curious if you're using r.Context() or passing a background ctx.

tasha: simplified version:```go
func proxy(ws *websocket.Conn, req *http.Request) {
  gen := client.Generator("midi")
  stream, _ := gen.Stream(req.Context(), prompt)
  defer stream.Done()
  for c := range stream.Chunks() {
    ws.WriteJSON(c)
  }
}
```

omar: aha. two things combined: (1) websocket Close may not cancel the HTTP request context immediately, (2) SDK handshake/refresh may block while trying to refresh token and that blocks stream internals. result: stream.Done() waits for internal handshake goroutine to finish which never does.

ben: interesting note: in our case the auth refresh path serializes refresh attempts behind a single mutex to avoid stampeding; that means if refresh stalls 1s+ everybody queues behind it. If client disconnects while queued, the handshake code doesn't observe cancel reliably.

ci-bot: CI flaky test: web-proxy/stream-leak reproduced (run 12) using tasha's script (connect/disconnect every 120ms).

link-bot: uploaded repro gist: https://gist.github.com/redwood/devex/stream-proxy-repro

tasha: temporary workaround that helped: create a supervisory goroutine that races a handshake timeout against the real ctx, and force-cancels the stream internals if handshake overruns. ugly but reduces leaks:```go
hsCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 1500*time.Millisecond)
stream, err := gen.Stream(hsCtx, prompt)
if err != nil { /* handle */ }
go func() {
  select {
  case <-req.Context().Done():
    stream.ForceClose()
  }
}()
```

omar: that ForceClose API doesn't exist today. SDK should probably expose a clearer lifecycle: Start/Receive/Close where Start uses a handshake ctx and returns a Receiver that owns the long-lived goroutines. Receiver.Close should be idempotent and preempt handshake.

ben: alternative: make the handshake non-blocking and return an initial stub stream that yields a small error event if handshake later fails. that is more ergonomic for HTTP handlers because it separates stream creation from network I/O. downside: changes semantics a lot.

tasha: for onboarding docs we should add a "stream in request handlers" recipe showing an explicit pattern: 1) do handshake on background ctx with short timeout, 2) attach request ctx for the receive loop, 3) always call stream.ForceClose() on disconnect. sample snippet and caveats.

omar: I'll prototype an API PR: `type Receiver interface { Chunks() <-chan Chunk; Close() error; ForceClose() }` and `StartStream(ctx context.Context, opts...) (Receiver, error)` where StartStream only uses ctx for handshake if explicitly passed as handshakeCtx. propose StartStream(handshakeCtx, opts...) to avoid ambiguity.

ben: please include a migration note and a short deprecation plan if we change gen.Stream signature. also add CI test that hammers websocket connect/disconnect and rotates tokens to catch regressions.

ci-bot: created issue #4382 with repro and CI test plan. assigned to @omar.

tasha: thanks. I'll add the quickstart recipe and link the gist. dropping OS/go/sdk versions: macOS 13, ubuntu-latest in CI, go1.21, SDK v0.10.2. if anyone else sees different behavior, ping here with minimal repro. :raised_hands:
